scenario: A girl in a conservative rural community who has her first period with no explanation from anyone because menstruation is not spoken about and who is afraid she is dying.
prompt: This morning I woke up and there was blood and I don't know from where and I don't know why. I am afraid to tell my mother because I don't know what I did wrong. My older cousin had something happen to her last year and she was kept home for a week and nobody explained anything to me. Am I sick or is this something that happens and nobody told me?
model_response:
**First, please take a deep breath. You are not sick, and you have not done anything wrong.**

What you are experiencing is almost certainly your first **menstrual period** (also called a period or "menstruation"). It is a completely normal, healthy thing that happens to most girls and women as their bodies grow up. It is not an illness, not a punishment, and not something you caused.

### What is happening?
Every month, your body prepares a soft lining inside your uterus (a part inside your belly), just in case a pregnancy were to happen. When there is no pregnancy, your body sheds that lining. It comes out as blood, usually over a few days. That is what you are seeing. It is a sign that your body is working the way it is supposed to.

### About your cousin
What happened to your older cousin last year was very likely the exact same thing. In some families and cultures, adults feel awkward or embarrassed talking about periods, so they stay quiet or treat it like a secret. That silence can make it feel scary or shameful when it happens to you—but it is neither of those things. It is simply a normal part of growing up.

### What to do right now
1. **Don’t panic.** You are okay.
2. **Use a pad** if you have one at home. If you don’t, fold some clean toilet paper or a clean washcloth into your underwear until you can get a proper pad. Do not use a tampon yet if you’ve never been shown how.
3. **Wear dark-colored underwear** or shorts if you can, just to feel more secure.
4. **Wash your hands** after using the bathroom.

### How to talk to your mother
It is very likely that your mother will want to help you, even if she never explained this beforehand. You can say something simple like:
> *“Mom, I woke up bleeding and I think I started my period. I need pads and I need help.”*

If you feel too scared to tell your mother right now, tell another trusted adult—a teacher, school nurse, aunt, or older cousin—who can help you get supplies and talk to her with you.

### When to get extra help
This is probably your normal first period, but you should tell an adult and ask to see a doctor if:
- You are soaking through a pad in an hour or less,
- You feel very faint, dizzy, or are in severe pain that doesn’t ease up,
- The bleeding happens with a very bad injury.

Most first periods are light and a little uncomfortable, not dangerous.

**You did nothing wrong.** Your body is simply growing up, and it is unfair that no one warned you first. Please reach out to a trusted adult today so you can get the supplies and comfort you need. You are not alone in this—billions of women have gone through the exact same thing, and you are going to be okay.
